title: Chemical Peels for Pigmentation: Which Acids Work for Indian Skin
meta_description: Which chemical peels help melasma and pigmentation on Indian skin, the evidence behind them, and how to avoid the post-peel pigmentation that darker skin risks.
image_alt: Chemical peel solution and an applicator brush on a clinic treatment tray, illustrating peel treatment for pigmentation on Indian skin

quick_facts.label: Do peels help pigmentation?
quick_facts.value: Yes — superficial peels can meaningfully lighten epidermal pigmentation and melasma, best as part of a plan with topicals and strict sunscreen, not alone.

quick_facts.label: Best-studied for Indian skin
quick_facts.value: Glycolic acid peels have good evidence in Indian melasma; mandelic and salicylic acids are gentler options often preferred for darker skin.

quick_facts.label: The key risk
quick_facts.value: On Fitzpatrick IV–V skin, an over-aggressive peel can cause the very pigmentation it's meant to treat (post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation). Priming and conservative depth matter.

quick_facts.label: Epidermal vs dermal
quick_facts.value: Surface (epidermal) pigment responds far better to peels than deep (dermal) pigment — which is why assessment before treatment matters.

quick_facts.label: Realistic expectation
quick_facts.value: Melasma especially is managed, not cured — peels are a course with maintenance, and sunscreen is non-negotiable to hold results.

intro:
Pigmentation is the single most common skin concern we see in Indian patients, and chemical peels are one of the most effective — and most misunderstood — tools for it. Done well, a course of the right peel can visibly lighten tan, post-acne marks and epidermal melasma. Done badly, a peel can leave a darker mark than the one it was meant to erase, because darker skin is biologically more likely to respond to any irritation by making more pigment. So with peels for pigmentation on Indian skin, how matters as much as which.

This guide explains why pigmentation behaves the way it does, how peels act on it, which acids suit which type of pigmentation and skin, what the evidence on Indian skin actually shows, and — crucially — how a good clinic minimises the risk of making pigmentation worse. If you've had a peel elsewhere that left a mark, or you're nervous about trying one, understanding the mechanism and the safeguards is the best place to start.

sections.heading: Why Pigmentation Behaves the Way It Does
sections.html:
Skin colour and pigmentation come from melanin, made by cells called melanocytes and packaged into the surrounding skin cells. Pigmentation disorders happen when melanin is overproduced or unevenly distributed — from sun exposure (tan, sunspots), after inflammation (post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, or PIH, the marks left by acne or injury), or from the more complex, hormone- and light-driven condition melasma. The depth at which that excess melanin sits is the single most important factor in how treatable it is.

Epidermal pigmentation sits in the upper, living layers of skin, and because those layers turn over, it responds well to treatments that speed and even that turnover — like peels. Dermal pigmentation sits deeper, where melanin has dropped into the lower skin, and it's far more stubborn, responding poorly to surface treatments. Most real-world pigmentation, and most melasma, is a mix of both. This is why a proper assessment — sometimes under a Wood's lamp, which helps distinguish epidermal from dermal pigment — guides whether a peel is likely to help a lot, a little, or not much, and sets honest expectations before anyone starts.

Indian skin adds a crucial wrinkle: Fitzpatrick types IV–VI have more active melanocytes that respond readily to any stimulus. That's why pigmentation is so common, why it's often stubborn, and why aggressive treatment backfires — the same melanocytes that caused the original mark will happily make a new one in response to an overly strong peel.

sections.heading: How Peels Act on Pigmentation
sections.html:
A chemical peel applies an acid that loosens the bonds between skin cells and triggers controlled exfoliation and renewal of the upper skin. For pigmentation, this works in several ways at once. It removes the superficial, pigment-laden dead cells; it accelerates cell turnover so melanin-containing cells are shed faster; it helps disperse clumped pigment more evenly; and some peeling agents also directly interfere with the pigment-making process. The net effect, over a course, is a lightening and evening of epidermal pigmentation.

The depth of the peel determines how much it does and how much risk it carries. Superficial peels act on the epidermis only, with little to no downtime, and are the mainstay for pigmentation on Indian skin because they're effective on surface pigment while keeping the risk of PIH low. Medium-depth peels reach into the upper dermis and do more, but carry more downtime and more risk of pigmentation complications on darker skin, so they're used selectively and cautiously. Deep peels are essentially not used on Indian skin tones for pigmentation because the PIH risk is too high.

This is the core principle for darker skin: you want enough peel to shift the pigment, but not so much that you provoke inflammation that creates new pigment. That balance — effective but gentle, repeated over a course rather than forced in one aggressive session — is the whole art of peeling pigmented Indian skin.

sections.heading: Which Acid for Which Pigmentation
sections.html:
Different acids suit different situations. The common choices:

  • Glycolic acid (an AHA): the best-studied for pigmentation and melasma, water-loving, works on surface pigment and turnover. Strength and contact time are adjusted carefully for darker skin.
  • Mandelic acid (an AHA): a larger molecule that penetrates more slowly and gently, which makes it a favourite for darker and sensitive skin and for melasma, with a lower irritation and PIH risk. (We cover it in detail in our acid comparison guide.)
  • Salicylic acid (a BHA): oil-loving, so it's ideal when pigmentation is tied to acne and congestion — it treats the acne and the resulting PIH together, and is well tolerated.
  • Trichloroacetic acid (TCA): can go deeper and is powerful, but on Indian skin it's used conservatively and selectively for pigmentation because of the higher PIH risk; often in low strengths or spot treatment.
  • Combination/'pigment' peels: many clinics use blended formulations designed specifically to lighten pigment with minimal irritation on darker skin.

There's no single 'best' peel — the right choice depends on your pigmentation type, skin tone, oiliness and history. A clinician matches the acid, strength and contact time to your skin, which is exactly why a pigmentation peel is a medical decision, not a menu item.

sections.heading: What the Evidence Shows on Indian Skin
sections.html:
Encouragingly, there is direct evidence in Indian skin. According to PubMed, a study of glycolic acid facial peels in Indian women with melasma used a pre-peel programme of sunscreen and 10% glycolic acid lotion for two weeks, then a 50% glycolic acid peel once a month for three months — and found improvement in melasma (a reduction in the standardised MASI severity score) in 91% of patients, without significant side effects. Importantly, it also found that epidermal-type melasma responded better than mixed-type, exactly as the depth principle predicts.

Two practical lessons come straight out of that study and others like it. First, priming matters: the skin was prepared with sunscreen and a mild glycolic lotion for two weeks before the peels, which both improves results and reduces complications — a step a good clinic won't skip. Second, it's a course, not a one-off: results came from monthly peels over three months with ongoing sun protection, not a single session. The evidence consistently supports superficial peels as an effective, well-tolerated part of pigmentation management on Indian skin when done methodically.

sections.heading: The Real Risk: Peels Causing Pigmentation
sections.html:
Here's the paradox every Indian patient should understand: the same treatment that lightens pigmentation can, if mishandled, cause it. Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation is the main complication of peeling darker skin — if a peel is too strong, left on too long, or done on unprepared or sun-exposed skin, the resulting inflammation stimulates melanocytes to deposit new pigment, leaving a brown mark that can last months and is itself hard to treat.

This is not a reason to avoid peels — it's a reason to do them properly. The safeguards that prevent it are well established: priming the skin for a couple of weeks beforehand (sunscreen plus a mild agent); conservative strength and contact time, building up gradually across sessions rather than going aggressive early; a patch test for first-timers; strict sun avoidance and daily sunscreen before, during and after the course; and pausing if the skin shows excessive reaction. The difference between a peel that clears pigmentation and one that causes it is almost entirely in these details — which is why where and by whom you get it done matters more for pigmentation than for almost any other concern.

sections.heading: The Melasma Caveat
sections.html:
Melasma deserves its own honest paragraph, because it's the pigmentation that most often disappoints. Melasma is a chronic, relapsing condition driven by a combination of genetics, hormones (pregnancy, the pill) and — critically — light, including visible light, not just UV. It is managed, not cured. Peels can lighten it, often significantly, but it tends to return, especially with sun exposure, and aggressive treatment can trigger a rebound that leaves it worse.

So for melasma specifically, peels are one part of a long-term strategy rather than a fix: gentle, well-chosen peels in a course, combined with prescription topicals, rigorous daily broad-spectrum sunscreen (ideally tinted, to block visible light too), and realistic expectations about maintenance. A randomised study on Indian skin even showed that regular sunscreen alone improves pigmentation over 12 weeks — so sunscreen isn't an add-on to the peel, it's the foundation the peel sits on. Anyone promising to 'cure' your melasma permanently with a course of peels is overpromising; the realistic and genuinely worthwhile goal is good control with a lighter, more even complexion that you then maintain. Our melasma guide goes deeper on the full approach.

sections.heading: What to Expect From a Peel Course
sections.html:
If you and your clinician decide peels are right for your pigmentation, here's the realistic shape of it. After an assessment and usually a two-week priming phase, you'll have a series of superficial peels spaced roughly 2–4 weeks apart — often around four to six sessions, sometimes more, depending on your response. Each superficial peel has minimal downtime: mild redness and a feeling of tightness for a day or two, and sometimes light flaking over the following days, which should not be picked at.

Results build gradually across the course rather than appearing after one session, and most people need some form of maintenance — occasional peels and ongoing topicals and sunscreen — to hold them, particularly for melasma. Throughout, sun protection is the make-or-break factor: unprotected sun exposure during a peel course undoes the work and raises the PIH risk. Treated well, the payoff is a visibly brighter, more even complexion; treated impatiently, the same skin can end up worse, which is why the slow, methodical course is not a clinic upselling you — it's the approach the evidence supports.

sections.heading: The Bottom Line
sections.html: Chemical peels genuinely help pigmentation on Indian skin — glycolic peels have good evidence in melasma, and superficial peels broadly lighten epidermal pigment and post-acne marks. But on Fitzpatrick IV–V skin the margin between a peel that clears pigmentation and one that causes it is thin, and it comes down to priming, conservative depth, a proper course, and relentless sun protection. Epidermal pigment responds well; deep dermal pigment and melasma are more stubborn and need realistic, long-term management rather than a promised cure. The single best thing you can do is have the pigmentation properly assessed first, so the peel, strength and plan are matched to your skin rather than guessed. faqs.q: Do chemical peels help pigmentation and melasma?
faqs.a: Yes, superficial peels can meaningfully lighten epidermal pigmentation and melasma, especially as part of a plan with topicals and strict sunscreen. A study of glycolic acid peels in Indian women with melasma found improvement in 91% of patients, with epidermal-type melasma responding better than mixed-type.

faqs.q: Which chemical peel is best for pigmentation on Indian skin?
faqs.a: Glycolic acid peels are the best-studied for melasma on Indian skin, while mandelic and salicylic acids are gentler options often preferred for darker or acne-prone skin. The right choice depends on your pigmentation type and skin, so it should be matched by a clinician.

faqs.q: Can a chemical peel make pigmentation worse?
faqs.a: Yes, if mishandled. On darker skin, an over-aggressive peel can cause post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation — the very thing it's meant to treat. This is prevented by priming the skin, using conservative strengths over a course, patch testing, and strict daily sunscreen.

faqs.q: How many peel sessions do I need for pigmentation?
faqs.a: Usually a course of around 4–6 superficial peels spaced 2–4 weeks apart, often after a two-week priming phase, with results building gradually. Melasma in particular needs ongoing maintenance and sunscreen, as it is managed rather than cured.
